answer.line: Fixation is the step that pulls N2 out of the air and turns it into ammonia.

steps: Start in the air. N2 is most of the atmosphere, but its triple bond keeps almost every organism from using it.
Fixation is the one step that breaks that bond: bacteria with nitrogenase turn N2 into NH3.
Every other choice starts from nitrogen that is already fixed, so it comes later. Each one is a numbered step in the picture.

choices.note: That is nitrification: soil bacteria oxidize ammonia to nitrite, then nitrate. It starts from nitrogen fixation already delivered.
That is denitrification. It sends nitrogen back to the air, the opposite of fixation, which brings it in.
Nitrogenase in bacteria, free living or in root nodules, breaks the triple bond and makes ammonia.

choices.text: NH₄⁺ to amino acids in plant tissue
choices.note: That is assimilation: a plant builds fixed nitrogen into its own amino acids. Fixation had to happen first.
That is ammonification: decomposers free ammonium from dead matter. It recycles nitrogen already in living things.

lockIt: Fixation is the only way in from the air: N2 to NH3.

legend.label: Fixation: bacteria turn N2 into ammonia
Nitrification: NH4+ to NO2- to NO3-
Assimilation: plants build nitrate or ammonium into amino acids
Ammonification: decomposers free NH4+ from dead matter
Denitrification: NO3- back to N2 gas

visual.alt: The nitrogen cycle as five boxes joined by numbered arrows: N2 gas in the air, ammonia in the soil, nitrite, nitrate, and organic nitrogen in living things. Arrow 1, fixation from N2 to ammonia, is drawn in green and named the answer in the legend. The other arrows are nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification, one for each trap.
visual.caption: Every choice is a numbered step here. Only arrow 1 starts in the air.
